items.prompt: In an unweighted graph, why does the first BFS discovery of vertex v establish its minimum number of edges from source s?

options.text: Queues are faster than stacks, so the first route found must be shortest.
Every graph becomes a tree before BFS begins, so each vertex has only one possible path.
The FIFO frontier processes vertices in nondecreasing distance layers, so any later discovery route is no shorter.
BFS is shortest only when edge lookup uses an adjacency matrix.

feedback.reason: FIFO processing preserves nondecreasing edge distance from the source.

blocks.text: FIFO preserves complete distance layers

items: Initialize s at distance 0 and enqueue it.
When BFS removes a vertex u at distance d, every earlier queue entry has distance at most d and every newly added neighbor receives d + 1.
FIFO places those d + 1 neighbors behind all already-pending vertices from distance d or d + 1.
Therefore BFS cannot process a longer layer before a shorter one.

blocks.text: If v is first discovered from u at distance d, the path used has d + 1 edges. Any path with fewer edges would have a predecessor in an earlier layer, which BFS would already have processed and used to discover v. Marking v on discovery fixes that minimum and prevents duplicate frontier entries.

blocks.title: Proof boundary
blocks.text: First discovery is minimum only when every edge contributes the same unit cost and the frontier is FIFO by discovery.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.queue_speed: Data-structure speed does not prove optimality; the distance-layer invariant does.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_lookup: The guarantee depends on equal edge cost and FIFO layering, not on a specific representation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_assumption: The graph may contain cycles and multiple paths; the BFS discovery tree is created during search.

items.prompt: Order the actions for handling one candidate neighbor v while processing vertex u in canonical BFS. v is currently undiscovered.

elements.text: Confirm that v has not been discovered.
Append v to the FIFO queue.

feedback.reason: BFS must claim v before another predecessor can enqueue it.

blocks.text: Claim, label, then expose the neighbor

items: Check that v is not already discovered.
Mark v discovered immediately, reserving its single canonical frontier entry.
Set distance[v] = distance[u] + 1 from the layer that first reached it.
Enqueue v so it can later expand its own neighbors.

blocks.text: If two vertices in the current layer both point to v, marking before enqueue makes the second edge observe v as already claimed. Marking only when v is later dequeued would allow both predecessors to enqueue a copy. Setting the distance and marking can be one implementation operation, but both precede frontier exposure.

blocks.title: Neighbor invariant
blocks.text: Every enqueued vertex is already discovered and already has its final unweighted distance.

items.prompt: BFS processes u with distance 4 and discovers an unvisited neighbor v through edge u → v in an unweighted graph. What distance should be assigned at discovery?

options.text: Leave it unknown until the queue is empty.
Use the row index from the adjacency matrix instead of u’s distance.

feedback.reason: An unweighted edge contributes exactly one additional step from the source.

blocks.text: One unweighted edge adds one to distance
The known path from s to u contains 4 edges. Appending the edge u → v creates a path to v with 4 + 1 = 5 edges, so BFS assigns distance[v] = 5 when v is first discovered.

blocks.title: Why the other values fail
blocks.text: Distance 4 omits the newly traversed edge. Waiting until the queue is empty discards the first-discovery guarantee, and an adjacency-matrix row index is a vertex-storage coordinate, not a path length.

blocks.title: Local update
blocks.text: For an undiscovered unweighted neighbor v, assign distance[v] = distance[u] + 1 at discovery.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.distance_four: Traversing one edge increases the edge-count distance by one.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.distance_unknown: The layer invariant permits a final minimum distance at first discovery in an unweighted graph.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.distance_matrix: Vertex identifiers and storage positions are not path lengths.

items.prompt: A road graph has positive travel times on edges: one direct edge s → t costs 100, while s → a and a → t each cost 10. Why is ordinary BFS not a valid minimum-travel-time algorithm?

options.text: BFS is invalid because DFS is always faster on weighted graphs.
BFS would become valid after changing the adjacency list to a matrix.
Marking t only when dequeued makes the direct edge’s cost reconsidered correctly.
BFS minimizes edge count, but edge count no longer matches total travel time.

feedback.reason: One edge is not one unit of objective cost, so FIFO edge layers do not order states by travel time.

blocks.text: Edge layers and cost layers disagree

items: The direct route s → t has one edge but total travel time 100.
The route s → a → t has two edges but total travel time 10 + 10 = 20.
Ordinary BFS reaches the one-edge layer first, so first discovery favors cost 100 even though 20 is smaller.

blocks.text: Changing graph storage or visited timing does not compare accumulated costs. With nonnegative edge weights, Dijkstra's algorithm uses a priority frontier ordered by tentative total distance and relaxes an edge when it finds a cheaper route.

blocks.title: Transfer boundary
blocks.text: Ordinary BFS minimizes edge count, not an arbitrary sum of positive edge weights.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_too_slow: Neither DFS nor ordinary BFS solves positive weighted shortest paths by a universal speed rule.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_missing: Representation does not restore the equal-cost premise required by BFS distance layers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visit_on_dequeue: Visited timing alone does not perform weighted distance relaxation or compare accumulated costs.

items.prompt: A BFS must traverse a sparse graph. Which statement correctly separates traversal mechanics from representation cost?

options.text: A matrix is invalid for BFS, not merely more expensive on a sparse graph.
BFS is O(V + E) under every representation because the queue is FIFO.
With adjacency lists, a full traversal is O(V + E); with a matrix, scanning neighbor rows can make it O(V²).
Switching to DFS guarantees a lower asymptotic cost.

feedback.reason: BFS controls frontier order, while the representation controls how neighbors are enumerated.

blocks.text: Frontier work and neighbor-access work add together

items: Mark-on-discovery gives each vertex at most one enqueue and one dequeue, for O(V) frontier operations in a full traversal.
With adjacency lists, the lengths of all scanned neighbor lists sum to O(E), or O(2E) entries for an undirected graph, which is still O(E).
With a V × V matrix, each reached vertex scans an entire V-cell row, so a full traversal can take O(V²).

blocks.text: FIFO order defines BFS semantics but does not make neighbor enumeration free. A matrix can still represent and traverse the graph correctly; it is simply a poor sparse-graph cost match here. DFS under the same representation scans the same neighbor storage and does not automatically lower the asymptotic bound.

blocks.title: Cost rule
blocks.text: BFS time equals canonical frontier operations plus the representation's total neighbor-enumeration cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_always_linear: A matrix may scan V possible neighbors for each reached vertex, so representation changes the neighbor-enumeration cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_always_wrong: A matrix can represent the graph correctly; the issue here is its cost profile, not correctness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dfs_faster: Under the same representation, full BFS and DFS usually inspect the same vertices and edge entries.

items.prompt: BFS starts at vertex 0 in a graph where vertices {0,1,2} form one component and {3,4} form another. What will one correct BFS invocation visit?

options.text: All five vertices because BFS expands by global layers.
Only {0,1,2}, the vertices reachable from 0.
All five only if the graph uses an adjacency matrix.
All five because the BFS tree automatically adds roots for unseen vertices.

feedback.reason: A BFS invocation is bounded by paths from its source.

blocks.text: A source queue cannot cross a missing path

items: Enqueue source 0.
Edges inside its component can discover 1 and 2.
After 0, 1, and 2 are processed, the queue is empty.
Neither 3 nor 4 was reachable from 0, so neither ever entered this invocation's queue.

blocks.text: The visited result is exactly {0,1,2}. Global layers are still relative to a source and cannot bridge disconnected components. A whole-graph task needs an outer vertex scan that starts another BFS from an unseen vertex such as 3.

blocks.title: Invocation scope
blocks.text: One BFS visits one source's reachable set, independent of representation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_vertices: Layers are measured within the reachable region; BFS cannot cross a missing edge between components.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_all: A representation cannot create reachability between vertices that have no connecting path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_all: One BFS tree has one source; a whole-graph outer loop is needed to start another tree.

items.prompt: The task asks only whether t is reachable from s. Which comparison between BFS and DFS is justified?

options.text: BFS is always correct and faster, while DFS is not a graph-reachability algorithm.
DFS is valid only because recursion follows tree rules and needs no visited set.
They are equivalent only if both delay visited marking until removal from their frontier.
Both are valid with cycle-safe visited state; choose from required order, memory, and implementation constraints.

feedback.reason: Reachability needs complete exploration, so both traversal orders are correct under the same visited contract.

blocks.text: Both orders preserve the reachable-set contract

items: BFS uses a FIFO queue and explores by edge-distance layers.
DFS uses recursion or a LIFO stack and follows one branch before siblings.
With cycle-safe discovery and adjacency lists, both inspect the reached vertices and edges in O(Vr + Er).

blocks.text: Because the prompt asks only whether t is reachable, either complete traversal may stop when t is found or fail when its frontier empties. BFS adds a minimum-unweighted-distance guarantee that is unnecessary here; DFS can face deep recursion, while BFS can retain a wide layer. These are workload and implementation trade-offs, not a universal speed ranking.

blocks.title: Choose from the output contract
blocks.text: Use either traversal for reachability; require BFS when layer order or minimum unweighted distance is part of the result.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_always: DFS is a standard reachability traversal; neither has a universal speed advantage for full exploration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dfs_no_visited: The input graph may have cycles; recursion does not convert it into a tree before discovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dequeue_same: Both need a correct discovery invariant; late unguarded marking can duplicate work.

items.prompt: Two different shortest paths reach v at the same BFS distance. The first discovered predecessor is p1, but another predecessor p2 is processed later in the same layer. What is the canonical single-parent behavior?

options.text: Always replace p1 with p2 because later queue entries are more accurate.
Keep p1 if only one shortest path must be reconstructed; v’s minimum distance is already final.
Enqueue v again from p2 so BFS can decide after both copies are dequeued.
This situation is impossible because a BFS tree proves the input graph has one path per vertex.

feedback.reason: First discovery fixes the minimum distance; a single-parent reconstruction may retain the first valid predecessor.

blocks.text: One-parent reconstruction chooses one shortest-path witness

items: p1 first discovers v and sets distance[v] to distance[p1] + 1.
The same discovery stores parent[v] = p1 and enqueues v once.
When p2 later exposes an equal-distance edge to v, v is already discovered, so canonical single-parent BFS keeps p1.

blocks.text: The edge from p2 proves a second shortest predecessor, not a more accurate one. Replacing p1 arbitrarily changes the chosen witness, and re-enqueueing v weakens the one-discovery invariant without improving distance. If the output requires every shortest path or their count, retain all predecessors satisfying distance[p] + 1 = distance[v], or accumulate counts under that condition.

blocks.title: State follows output
blocks.text: Keep the first parent for one shortest path; store additional equal-distance predecessor evidence only when the output requires it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.replace_later: Both predecessors produce the same minimum distance; later discovery is not more accurate by itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.enqueue_again: Duplicate enqueues are unnecessary for one shortest path and weaken the single-discovery invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_unique: The BFS tree selects one discovery edge; the original graph may have several shortest paths.

items.prompt: A BFS must return one shortest path from s to t, not every shortest path. Which per-vertex state is sufficient to reconstruct that path?

options.text: One parent pointer recorded when each vertex is first discovered.
Every walk reaching the vertex, including walks with repeated vertices.
Only the queue position at which the vertex is removed.
The number of adjacent vertices, without any predecessor information.

feedback.reason: BFS fixes a minimum distance at first discovery, so one discovery parent per vertex is enough for one witness path.

blocks.text: Follow parent[t] backward until s, then reverse the collected vertices. Storing every predecessor is necessary only when the output asks for all shortest paths or their count.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_walks: Enumerating walks is unnecessary and can be infinite in a cyclic graph.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.queue_position: Removal order does not identify which edge established the path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.neighbor_count: Degree contains no predecessor identity and cannot reconstruct a route.

items.prompt: If BFS only needs the minimum distance from s to target t, when is it safe to terminate the search?

options.text: When t is first discovered and assigned a distance.
Only after every reachable vertex has been processed.
Before the source is enqueued, because t may be adjacent.
As soon as any neighbor of s is inspected.

feedback.reason: FIFO layering makes the first discovery of t a minimum-distance discovery.

blocks.text: A later route can be equal in length but cannot be shorter, because every layer closer to s is processed before the layer that discovers t. Full traversal is required only for other outputs, such as all components.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.after_all: Completing the graph is unnecessary for a single target distance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.before_queue: The source must be initialized and processed before any reachable target can be discovered.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.on_any_neighbor: An arbitrary neighbor says nothing about the distance to t.

items.prompt: What can BFS layer parity help determine in an unweighted graph?

options.text: Whether edges can be checked for a two-coloring by alternating colors across layers.
The exact shortest path when edges have arbitrary weights.
A dependency order for every directed graph.
The vertices sorted by degree.

feedback.reason: Adjacent vertices in a BFS layering receive opposite parity colors in a bipartite check.

blocks.text: An edge joining two vertices with the same assigned parity proves an odd-cycle conflict. This use of BFS relies on unweighted adjacency layers, not edge-cost optimization.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.weighted_shortest: Parity does not encode arbitrary edge costs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.topological_order: Cycles and undirected parity are a different contract from dependency ordering.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.degree_sort: BFS order is not degree order.

items.prompt: How should BFS represent a vertex that remains undiscovered after the queue is exhausted?

options.text: Use the problem's explicit unreachable sentinel, such as infinity or -1.
Assign distance zero because no path was found.
Use the last queue position as its distance.
Copy the source distance to every undiscovered vertex.

feedback.reason: An undiscovered vertex has no path from the source, not a zero-length path.

blocks.text: Initialize distances to the contract's unavailable value and overwrite only on discovery. Do not infer reachability from the final queue length.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero: Zero is reserved for the source or an actual zero-distance state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.queue_index: Queue position is not graph distance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.source_distance: An unreachable vertex has no valid distance to copy.

items.prompt: If BFS must traverse an entire disconnected graph, what outer control flow is needed?

options.text: Scan all vertices and start BFS from each still-undiscovered vertex.
Run from one source and assume every vertex will enter the queue.
Clear visited state after every distance layer.
Sort vertices before enqueuing the first source.

feedback.reason: One BFS covers one reachable component; the outer loop supplies seeds for the rest.

blocks.text: Keep visited state across component searches so each vertex is classified once. This pattern supports component counts and full-graph traversal.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.single_source_only: A disconnected component has no path from the chosen source.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reset_each_layer: Resetting causes duplicate visits and incorrect distances.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_vertices: Vertex ordering does not create missing edges.

items.prompt: What can dominate BFS auxiliary space on a graph even when each vertex is enqueued only once?

options.text: A wide distance layer can place O(V) vertices in the queue at once.
Edge weights always make the queue exponential.
Sorting vertices adds no space but makes the queue infinite.
The queue is always O(1) because one vertex is removed at a time.

feedback.reason: Queue occupancy measures the active frontier, which can contain many vertices from the same layer.

blocks.text: Total traversal time is O(V+E) with adjacency lists, while auxiliary queue and visited state can each be O(V). Per-pop processing does not imply constant peak occupancy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.edge_weights: Weights do not by themselves make a FIFO queue exponential.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_input: Sorting is unrelated to queue occupancy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_only: A broad frontier can contain a linear number of vertices.

items.prompt: In unweighted BFS, what invariant holds when a vertex is first discovered?

options.text: Its assigned distance is the minimum number of edges from the source.
Its assigned distance is the longest possible walk from the source.
Its assigned distance equals its degree.
Its distance is unknown until every graph vertex is processed.

feedback.reason: FIFO layers discover vertices in nondecreasing edge distance.

blocks.text: All vertices at distance d are processed before any vertex at distance d+1 can discover a new state. Therefore the first assignment is already shortest under unit edge costs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.maximum: BFS does not optimize longest walks.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.degree: Degree is unrelated to distance from the source.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.final_only: A first discovery is sufficient for the shortest-distance invariant.

items.prompt: To reconstruct one shortest path after BFS, what should be recorded when a vertex is first discovered?

options.text: The predecessor vertex that caused the discovery.
Every edge in the graph copied into the vertex record.
The queue length at the moment of discovery.
Only the final neighbor inspected before dequeue.

feedback.reason: A parent pointer preserves one witness predecessor for each discovered vertex.

blocks.text: Following parent pointers from the target back to the source yields one shortest path because the pointer was set on first minimum-distance discovery.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_edges: All edges are unnecessary for reconstructing one path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.queue_length: Queue occupancy does not identify the predecessor.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.last_neighbor: The final inspected neighbor may not be the discovering edge.

items.prompt: A BFS starts at s and the requested output is the distance to t, but t is in another component. What should the algorithm return?

options.text: The explicit unreachable result from the problem contract.
Zero, because no edges were traversed.
One, because t is a graph vertex.
Keep expanding the queue until t appears.

feedback.reason: No path exists between separate connected components.

blocks.text: Once the queue is empty without discovering t, the search has exhausted every vertex reachable from s. The result must use the specified unavailable sentinel or representation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero: Zero means the source itself or a valid zero-length route, not absence of a path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one: Vertex existence does not imply reachability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.continue_forever: A finite graph queue empties when the reachable component is exhausted.

items.prompt: Why must a BFS queue store vertices rather than only their distances?

options.text: The vertex identity is needed to retrieve and expand its neighbors.
Distance values uniquely identify which adjacency list to scan.
The degree is enough to determine every next vertex.
The source identity remains sufficient for all later expansions.

feedback.reason: Traversal state must identify the graph state whose neighbors are being expanded.

blocks.text: A distance is a label shared by many vertices. The queue entry needs the vertex identity, optionally paired with metadata such as distance or parent, to continue traversal.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.distance_only: Many vertices can share the same distance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.degree_only: Degree does not identify neighbor destinations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.source_only: Expansion moves through newly discovered vertices, not the source alone.
